name: Provenance of Research Images and Data
title: Provenance of Research Images and Data
answer: Provenance of research images and data is the record of where a dataset or image came from, how it was created or collected, who modified it, and under what conditions it can be reused. It covers raw experimental outputs, processed figures, microscopy images, clinical scans, survey data, and the metadata that ties them to instruments, protocols, and people. In AI research it also includes the lineage of training and evaluation data, because a model inherits the quality and biases of its sources. The goal is to make the chain from original observation to published result auditable.

sections.body: Provenance of research images and data is the record of where a dataset or image came from, how it was created or collected, who modified it, and under what conditions it can be reused. It covers raw experimental outputs, processed figures, microscopy images, clinical scans, survey data, and the metadata that ties them to instruments, protocols, and people. In AI research it also includes the lineage of training and evaluation data, because a model inherits the quality and biases of its sources. The goal is to make the chain from original observation to published result auditable.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Provenance tracking runs on a mix of laboratory information management systems, electronic lab notebooks, data repositories, and version control systems. Persistent identifiers such as DOIs and ORCID iDs link datasets, images, authors, and institutions. Cryptographic hashes and digital signatures can fix a file's state at a point in time, while metadata standards like Dublin Core or OME-XML carry the descriptive fields. In practice many research groups still rely on shared drives and spreadsheets, which makes automated provenance capture uneven.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by recording provenance at the point of creation rather than reconstructing it later. Instruments and software export raw files with embedded metadata, and researchers add protocol, sample, and analysis steps in structured logs. For images, this includes capture settings, processing operations, and any cropping, contrast adjustment, or annotation. For datasets, it includes collection method, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and any cleaning or transformation. Reviewers and auditors then compare the published figure or table against the logged chain to detect undisclosed manipulation or reuse.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance raises rights and risk questions about ownership, consent, licensing, and attribution. A dataset may contain personal data, protected health information, or copyrighted material, and its reuse depends on the terms under which it was originally obtained. Missing provenance makes it hard to know whether consent covers a new use, whether an image can be shared, or who should be credited. Research integrity policies increasingly require data availability statements and provenance metadata, but enforcement varies by field and publisher.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Provenance practice is moving toward automated capture, standardized provenance graphs, and machine-readable records that can be checked at scale. AI tools are being used to detect duplicated or altered images and to trace dataset lineage across papers, though they still need human review. Expect closer ties between preprint servers, journals, repositories, and funder systems so that a paper's claims can be linked to the exact data and code that support them. The long term goal is a research record where every image and dataset carries a verifiable history from acquisition to publication.
